title: Book 8, Chapter 26 — Twenty-first Year of the War—Recall of Alcibiades to Samos—Revolt of Euboea and Downfall of the Four Hundred—Battle of Cynossema
paragraphs: In the same summer, immediately after this, the Peloponnesians refused to fight with their combined fleet. They did not think themselves a match for the enemy, and they were at a loss where to find money for so many ships, especially as Tissaphernes proved such a bad paymaster. So they sent Clearchus, son of Ramphias, with forty ships to Pharnabazus, as the original instructions from Peloponnese had provided. Pharnabazus had invited them and was ready to furnish pay, and Byzantium had also sent them offers to revolt. These Peloponnesian ships put out into the open sea to escape the notice of the Athenians. A storm overtook them, and the majority, with Clearchus, got into Delos and afterwards went back to Miletus. From there Clearchus went by land to the Hellespont to take up the command. Ten of the ships, however, under the Megarian Helixus, made the passage to the Hellespont and brought about the revolt of Byzantium. When the commanders at Samos learned of this, they sent a squadron to guard the Hellespont against them, and an encounter took place before Byzantium between eight vessels on either side.

Meanwhile the chiefs at Samos, and especially Thrasybulus, had remained firmly resolved to recall Alcibiades from the moment he changed the government. At last, in an assembly, they won over the mass of the soldiers. The soldiers voted for the recall and amnesty of Alcibiades, and the chiefs sailed over to Tissaphernes and brought Alcibiades to Samos. They were convinced that their only chance of safety lay in Alcibiades drawing Tissaphernes away from the Peloponnesians and over to themselves. An assembly was then held. In it Alcibiades complained of his private misfortune in having been banished and lamented it. He spoke at great length on public affairs, raised their hopes for the future very high, and extravagantly magnified his own influence with Tissaphernes. His aims were to frighten the oligarchical government at Athens, to hasten the dissolution of the clubs, to increase his credit with the army at Samos and strengthen their own confidence, and finally to turn the enemy as strongly as possible against Tissaphernes and destroy the hopes they had placed in him. So Alcibiades held out to the army promises as extravagant as these: Tissaphernes had solemnly assured him that if he could only trust the Athenians, they would never go short of supplies while he had anything left, no, not even if he had to coin his own silver couch; and he would bring the Phoenician fleet, now at Aspendus, to the Athenians instead of to the Peloponnesians. But he could trust the Athenians only if Alcibiades were recalled to be his security for them.

The Athenians heard this and much more besides, and at once elected him general together with the former ones and put all their affairs into his hands. Now there was not a man in the army who would have given up his present hopes of safety and of vengeance upon the Four Hundred for any consideration whatever. After what they had been told, they were inclined to look down on the enemy before them and to sail at once for Piraeus. Alcibiades flatly refused the plan of sailing for Piraeus and leaving their more immediate enemies behind them, although many insisted on it. He said that, now that he had been elected general, he would first sail to Tissaphernes and agree with him on measures for carrying on the war. So he left the assembly and departed immediately. He wished it to be thought that there was complete confidence between them, and he also wished to increase his standing with Tissaphernes and to show that he was now elected general and in a position to do him good or harm as he chose. In this way he managed to frighten the Athenians with Tissaphernes and Tissaphernes with the Athenians.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesians at Miletus heard of the recall of Alcibiades. They already distrusted Tissaphernes, and now they became far more disgusted with him than ever. After their refusal to go out and give battle to the Athenians when they appeared before Miletus, Tissaphernes had grown slacker than ever in his payments. Even before that, his unpopularity had been growing on account of Alcibiades. The soldiers gathered together, as before, and some persons of standing besides the soldiers began to reckon up their grievances. They had never yet received their pay in full; what they did receive was small, and even that was paid irregularly. Unless they fought a decisive battle or moved to some station where they could get supplies, the crews of the ships would desert. And it was all the fault of Astyochus, who indulged Tissaphernes for his own private advantage.

The army was engaged in these reflections when the following disturbance took place concerning the person of Astyochus. Most of the Syracusan and Thurian sailors were freemen, and these crews, the freest in the armament, were also the boldest in attacking Astyochus and demanding their pay. He answered them somewhat stiffly and threatened them. When Dorieus spoke up for his own sailors, Astyochus even went so far as to lift his baton against him. The mass of the men saw this and, in sailor fashion, rushed in a fury to strike Astyochus. He saw them in time, however, and fled for refuge to an altar, and so they were parted without his being struck. Meanwhile the Milesians surprised and took the fort that Tissaphernes had built in Miletus and turned out the garrison. This act met with the approval of the rest of the allies, and in particular of the Syracusans, but it found no favor with Lichas. He said, moreover, that the Milesians and the rest in the King’s country ought to show reasonable submission to Tissaphernes and pay him court until the war should be happily settled. The Milesians were angry with him for this and for other things of the kind, and when he afterwards died of sickness, they would not allow him to be buried where the Lacedaemonians with the army wished.

The discontent of the army with Astyochus and Tissaphernes had reached this pitch when Mindarus arrived from Lacedaemon to succeed Astyochus as admiral and took over the command. Astyochus now set sail for home. Tissaphernes sent with him one of his confidants, Gaulites, a Carian, who spoke the two languages. Gaulites was to complain of the Milesians for the affair of the fort and at the same time to defend Tissaphernes against the Milesians, who, as he knew, were on their way to Sparta chiefly to denounce his conduct. They had Hermocrates with them, who was to accuse Tissaphernes of joining with Alcibiades to ruin the Peloponnesian cause and of playing a double game. Indeed Hermocrates had always been at enmity with him because the pay was not restored in full. Eventually Hermocrates was banished from Syracuse, and new commanders — Potamis, Myscon, and Demarchus — came out to Miletus to the ships of the Syracusans. Tissaphernes then pressed harder than ever upon him in his exile, and among other charges accused him of having once asked him for money and then, because he failed to get it, given himself out as his enemy.

While Astyochus, the Milesians and Hermocrates made sail for Lacedaemon, Alcibiades had crossed back from Tissaphernes to Samos. After his return, the envoys of the Four Hundred arrived from Delos. They had been sent, as mentioned above, to pacify the forces at Samos and explain matters to them. An assembly was held in which they tried to speak. At first the soldiers would not hear them and cried out to put to death the subverters of the democracy. At last, after some difficulty, they calmed down and gave them a hearing. The envoys then informed them that the recent change had been made to save the city, not to ruin it or deliver it to the enemy, for the Four Hundred had already had the opportunity of doing that when the enemy invaded the country during their government. They said that all the Five Thousand would have their proper share in the government, and that the relatives of their hearers had no outrage to complain of, as Chaereas had slanderously reported, nor any other ill treatment, but were all in undisturbed enjoyment of their property just as the soldiers had left them. They made a number of other statements besides, which had no better success with their angry listeners. Amid a host of different opinions, the one that found most favor was that of sailing to Piraeus. It was now that Alcibiades for the first time did the state a service, and one of the most signal kind. The Athenians at Samos were bent upon sailing against their countrymen, and in that case Ionia and the Hellespont would most certainly have passed at once into the enemy’s hands. Alcibiades was the man who prevented them. At that moment no other man could have held back the multitude, but he stopped the intended expedition. He rebuked the resentment felt against the envoys on personal grounds and turned it aside. He dismissed them with an answer from himself: he did not object to the government of the Five Thousand, but he insisted that the Four Hundred be deposed and the Council of Five Hundred reinstated in power. Meanwhile any economies by which pay might be better provided for the armament had his entire approval. Generally, he bade them hold out and show a bold face to the enemy. If the city were saved, there was good hope that the two parties might some day be reconciled, whereas if either were once destroyed, that at Samos or that at Athens, there would no longer be anyone to be reconciled to. Meanwhile envoys arrived from the Argives, offering support to the Athenian commons at Samos. Alcibiades thanked them and dismissed them with a request to come when called upon. The Argives were accompanied by the crew of the Paralus. We left them placed in a troopship by the Four Hundred, with orders to cruise round Euboea. They had then been employed to carry some Athenian envoys sent by the Four Hundred — Laespodias, Aristophon, and Melesias — to Lacedaemon. As they sailed past Argos, they seized the envoys and handed them over to the Argives as the chief subverters of the democracy. Then, instead of returning to Athens, they took the Argive envoys on board and came to Samos in the galley that had been entrusted to them.

That same summer, the return of Alcibiades and the general conduct of Tissaphernes had driven the discontent of the Peloponnesians to its height, and they no longer doubted that he had gone over to the Athenians. Tissaphernes wished, it would seem, to clear himself of these charges. He prepared to go to Aspendus for the Phoenician fleet, and he asked Lichas to go with him, saying that Tamos would act as his lieutenant and provide pay for the armament while he was away. Accounts differ, and it is not easy to learn why he went to Aspendus and then did not bring the fleet after all. That one hundred and forty-seven Phoenician ships came as far as Aspendus is certain. Why they came no farther has been explained in different ways. Some say it was part of his plan to waste the Peloponnesian resources, since Tamos, his lieutenant, was no better and proved a worse paymaster than he was. Others say he brought the Phoenicians to Aspendus to extract money from them for their discharge, having never meant to use them. Others say it was because of the outcry against him at Lacedaemon: he wanted it said that the fault was not his, that the ships were really manned, and that he had certainly gone to fetch them. To myself it seems only too clear that he did not bring up the fleet because he wished to wear down and paralyze the Hellenic forces. The time lost on his journey to Aspendus would waste their strength, and by throwing his weight into neither scale he would keep them evenly balanced. If he had wished to end the war, he could have done so, provided that he came in a manner that left no room for doubt. Bringing up the fleet would in all probability have given the victory to the Lacedaemonians, whose navy, even as things stood, met the Athenian more as an equal than as an inferior. But what convicts him most plainly is the excuse he gave for not bringing the ships. He said that fewer had assembled than the King had ordered. Yet surely it would only have raised his credit if he had spent little of the King’s money and gained the same end at lower cost. Whatever his intention, Tissaphernes went to Aspendus and met the Phoenicians, and at his request the Peloponnesians sent a Lacedaemonian named Philip, with two galleys, to fetch the fleet.

Alcibiades learned that Tissaphernes had gone to Aspendus and sailed there himself with thirteen ships. He promised the Athenians at Samos a great and certain service: he would either bring the Phoenician fleet over to the Athenians or, at any rate, keep it from joining the Peloponnesians. In all probability he had known for some time that Tissaphernes never intended to bring the fleet. He wanted to compromise Tissaphernes as far as he could in the eyes of the Peloponnesians by his show of friendship toward himself and the Athenians, and so, in a manner, to force him to join their side.

Alcibiades weighed anchor and sailed east, straight for Phaselis and Caunus. Meanwhile the envoys whom the Four Hundred had sent to Samos reached Athens. They reported the message of Alcibiades: hold out, show a firm front to the enemy, and know that he had great hopes of reconciling them with the army and defeating the Peloponnesians. Most of the oligarchs were already discontented and only too ready to be quit of the business by any safe route, and this message greatly strengthened their resolve. They now formed a bloc and openly criticized the administration. Their leaders were some of the principal generals and officeholders under the oligarchy, such as Theramenes, son of Hagnon, and Aristocrates, son of Scellias, among others. These men were among the most prominent members of the government. They said they feared the army at Samos, and above all Alcibiades, and feared too that the envoys sent to Lacedaemon might harm the state without the people’s authority. They did not press their objection to the excessive concentration of power in a few hands, but they urged that the Five Thousand must be shown to exist in reality and not merely in name, and that the constitution must rest on a fairer footing. This, however, was only their political cry. Most of them were driven by private ambition, the very thing that most surely destroys oligarchies that grow out of democracies. For all such men at once claim to be not merely equals but each the chief and master of the rest. Under a democracy, by contrast, a defeated candidate accepts his defeat more easily, because he is not humiliated by losing to his equals. What most plainly encouraged the malcontents, though, was the power of Alcibiades at Samos and their own disbelief that the oligarchy would last. Each of them now raced the others to become the first leader of the commons.

Meanwhile the men among the Four Hundred who were most opposed to any form of democracy now redoubled their efforts. These were Phrynichus, who had quarreled with Alcibiades while commanding at Samos; Aristarchus, the bitter and inveterate enemy of the commons; Pisander and Antiphon; and others of the chiefs. Already, as soon as they entered upon power, and again when the army at Samos seceded from them and declared for a democracy, they had sent envoys from their own body to Lacedaemon and made every effort for peace, and they had built the wall in Eetionia. Now their envoys had come back from Samos, and they saw that not only the people but their own most trusted associates were turning against them. Alarmed at the state of things at Athens as well as at Samos, they sent off Antiphon and Phrynichus and ten others in haste, with instructions to make peace with Lacedaemon on any terms at all that were in any way tolerable. Meanwhile they pushed on the wall in Eetionia more actively than ever. According to Theramenes and his supporters, the purpose of this wall was not so much to keep out the army of Samos, in case it tried to force its way into Piraeus, as to be able to let in the fleet and army of the enemy at pleasure. For Eetionia is a mole of Piraeus, close alongside the entrance of the harbor. It was now fortified in connection with the wall already existing on the land side, so that a few men placed in it could command the entrance. The old wall on the land side and the new one now being built within on the side of the sea both ended in one of the two towers standing at the narrow mouth of the harbor. They also walled off the largest porch in Piraeus, which was directly connected with this wall, and kept it in their own hands. They compelled everyone to unload there the corn that came into the harbor, and what they had in stock, and to take it out from there when they sold it.

Theramenes had long murmured against these measures. When the envoys came back from Lacedaemon without having brought about any general peace, he declared that this wall was likely to ruin the state. At that moment forty-two ships from Peloponnese, among them some Siceliot and Italiot vessels from Locri and Tarentum, were riding off Las in Laconia, preparing for the voyage to Euboea; the Euboeans had invited them over. Their commander was Agesandridas, son of Agesander, a Spartan. Theramenes now declared that this squadron was meant less to aid Euboea than to aid the party fortifying Eetionia, and that unless precautions were taken quickly, the city would be surprised and lost. This was not mere slander, for the men he accused did in fact entertain some such plan. First, they wished to keep the oligarchy and not give up the empire. Failing that, they wished to keep their ships and walls and be independent. If this too were refused, they were resolved, rather than be the first victims of a restored democracy, to call in the enemy and make peace, surrender their walls and ships, and hold on to the government at all costs, so long as their own lives were safe.

For this reason they pressed on with building their work, complete with posterns, entrances and ways of bringing in the enemy, and they were eager to finish it in time. Meanwhile the murmurs against them were at first confined to a few persons and went on in secret. Then Phrynichus, who had come back from the embassy to Lacedaemon, was waylaid and stabbed in the crowded market by one of the Peripoli, and he dropped dead before he had gone far from the council chamber. The assassin escaped. His accomplice, an Argive, was captured, and the Four Hundred tortured him. They could get from him neither the name of his employer nor anything more than that he knew of many men who used to meet at the house of the commander of the Peripoli and at other houses. There the matter was allowed to drop. This gave so much courage to Theramenes, Aristocrates and the rest of their partisans, both inside the Four Hundred and outside it, that they decided to act. For by this time the ships had sailed round from Las and, anchoring at Epidaurus, had overrun Aegina. Theramenes argued that ships bound for Euboea would never have sailed in to Aegina and returned to anchor at Epidaurus, unless they had been invited to help the designs of which he had always accused the government. Further inaction was therefore impossible. In the end, after a great many seditious harangues and suspicions, they set to work in real earnest. Among the heavy infantry in Piraeus who were building the wall in Eetionia was Aristocrates, a colonel, with his own tribe. They seized Alexicles, a general under the oligarchy and a devoted adherent of the cabal, took him into a house and held him there. One Hermon, commander of the Peripoli in Munychia, and others helped them, and above all the great bulk of the heavy infantry was on their side. When the news reached the Four Hundred, who happened to be sitting in the council chamber, all except the disaffected wanted to go at once to the posts where the arms were kept, and they threatened Theramenes and his party. Theramenes defended himself, saying that he was ready to go at once and help rescue Alexicles. He took one of the generals of his party and went down to Piraeus, with Aristarchus and some young cavalrymen following. All was now panic and confusion. Those in the city imagined that Piraeus was already taken and the prisoner put to death, while those in Piraeus expected every moment to be attacked by the party in the city. The older men, however, stopped those who were running about the town and making for the stands of arms. Thucydides the Pharsalian, proxenus of the city, stepped forward and placed himself between the rival factions. He begged them not to ruin the state while the enemy was still near, waiting for his opportunity. In the end he succeeded in calming them and keeping their hands off each other. Meanwhile Theramenes, who was himself one of the generals, had come down to Piraeus and raged and stormed at the heavy infantry, while Aristarchus and the adversaries of the people were angry in real earnest. Most of the heavy infantry, however, went on with the business without faltering. They asked Theramenes whether he thought the wall had been built for any good purpose, and whether it would not be better to pull it down. He answered that if they thought it best to pull it down, he for his part agreed. At this the heavy infantry and a number of the people of Piraeus climbed straight onto the fortification and began to demolish it. Their cry to the multitude was that all who wished the Five Thousand to govern instead of the Four Hundred should join in the work. For instead of saying in so many words “all who wish the commons to govern,” they still disguised themselves under the name of the Five Thousand. They feared that the Five Thousand might really exist, and that a man might speak to one of them and get into trouble through ignorance. This, indeed, was why the Four Hundred did not want the Five Thousand to exist, and did not want it known that they did not exist. To give themselves so many partners in empire would, they thought, be downright democracy, while the uncertainty on the point would make the people afraid of one another.

On the next day the Four Hundred assembled in the council chamber, though they were alarmed. In Piraeus the heavy infantry set free their prisoner Alexicles and pulled down the fortification. They then marched under arms to the theater of Dionysus, close to Munychia, where they held an assembly and decided to march into the city. They set out and halted in the Anaceum. Delegates from the Four Hundred came to them there and argued with them man by man. These persuaded the most moderate they saw to stay quiet themselves and to hold back the rest. The delegates promised to make the Five Thousand known and to have the Four Hundred chosen from them in rotation, in whatever way the Five Thousand decided. In the meantime they begged the heavy infantry not to ruin the state or throw it into the arms of the enemy. Many men spoke and were spoken to, and the whole body of heavy infantry grew calmer than before, taken up with fear for the country as a whole. They agreed to hold an assembly in the theater of Dionysus on an appointed day, to restore concord.

The day came for the assembly in the theater, and they were on the point of gathering when news arrived that the forty-two ships under Agesandridas were sailing along the coast of Salamis from Megara. To a man the people took this to confirm what Theramenes and his party had so often said, that the ships were sailing to the fortification, and they decided that they had been right to pull it down. It may possibly have been by arrangement that Agesandridas lingered around Epidaurus and its neighborhood. But the hope of an opportunity arising from the troubles in the city would also naturally have kept him there. At any rate, the Athenians heard the news and at once ran down in a mass to Piraeus. They saw themselves threatened by the enemy with a worse war than their war among themselves, and one not far away but right at the harbor of Athens. Some boarded the ships that were already afloat, others launched new vessels, and others ran to defend the walls and the harbor mouth.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesian vessels sailed by, rounded Sunium, anchored between Thoricus and Prasiae, and afterwards arrived at Oropus. The Athenians had revolution in the city and were unwilling to lose a moment in going to the relief of their most important possession (for Euboea was everything to them now that they were shut out from Attica). They were compelled to put to sea in haste with untrained crews, and they sent Thymochares with some vessels to Eretria. On their arrival, these made up, with the ships already in Euboea, a total of thirty-six vessels, and they were forced to engage immediately. For Agesandridas, after his crews had dined, put out from Oropus, which is about seven miles from Eretria by sea. The Athenians saw him sailing up and immediately began to man their vessels. The sailors, however, instead of being by their ships, as the Athenians supposed, had gone off to buy provisions for their dinner in the houses on the outskirts of the town. The Eretrians had arranged that there should be nothing on sale in the marketplace, so that the Athenians would be a long time in manning their ships and, taken by surprise by the enemy’s attack, would be compelled to put to sea just as they were. A signal was also raised in Eretria to let the enemy in Oropus know when to put to sea. The Athenians, forced to put out so poorly prepared, engaged off the harbor of Eretria. They held their own for some little while notwithstanding, but were at length put to flight and chased to the shore. Those of them who took refuge in Eretria, which they presumed to be friendly to them, met their fate in that city, where the inhabitants butchered them. Those who fled to the Athenian fort in the Eretrian territory, and the vessels that got to Chalcis, were saved. The Peloponnesians took twenty-two Athenian ships, killed or took prisoner the crews, and set up a trophy. Not long afterwards they brought about the revolt of the whole of Euboea (except Oreus, which was held by the Athenians themselves) and made a general settlement of the affairs of the island.

When the news from Euboea reached Athens, the city fell into a panic worse than any it had known. Not even the disaster in Sicily, great as it had seemed at the time, nor anything else, had ever alarmed the Athenians so much. The camp at Samos was in revolt. They had no more ships, and no men to man them. They were divided among themselves and might at any moment come to blows. And now this great blow had fallen on top of everything else: they had lost their fleet and, worst of all, Euboea, which was worth more to them than Attica. Such a loss could not fail to throw them into the deepest despair. Their greatest and most immediate fear was that the enemy, emboldened by his victory, might sail straight for them and attack Piraeus, which they no longer had ships to defend. Every moment they expected him to arrive. With a little more courage he could easily have done it. Then he would either have deepened the dissensions of the city by his presence, or, if he had stayed to besiege it, he would have forced the fleet from Ionia to come to the rescue of their country and their relatives, even though it was hostile to the oligarchy. In the meantime he would have become master of the Hellespont, Ionia and the islands, and of everything as far as Euboea, or, to speak roundly, of the whole Athenian empire. But here, as on so many other occasions, the Lacedaemonians proved to be the most convenient people in the world for the Athenians to be at war with. The two peoples were very different in character: the Lacedaemonians were slow and lacking in energy, while their opponents were quick and enterprising. This difference was of the greatest service to Athens, especially as a maritime empire. The Syracusans proved it. They were the people most like the Athenians in character, and they were also the most successful in fighting them.

Nevertheless, as soon as the news arrived, the Athenians manned twenty ships and at once called a first assembly in the Pnyx, where they had formerly been used to meet. There they deposed the Four Hundred and voted to hand the government over to the Five Thousand. All who could furnish a suit of armor were to be members of this body. They also decreed that no one should receive pay for holding any office, and that anyone who did should be held accursed. Many other assemblies were held afterward, in which lawmakers were elected and every other measure was taken to form a constitution. It was during the first period of this constitution that the Athenians appear to have enjoyed the best government they ever had, at least in my time. The high and the low were combined with good judgment, and this is what first allowed the state to raise her head after her many disasters. They also voted to recall Alcibiades and other exiles. They sent word to him and to the camp at Samos, and urged them to devote themselves vigorously to the war.

As soon as this revolution took place, the party of Pisander and Alexicles and the chiefs of the oligarchs withdrew to Decelea. The one exception was Aristarchus, one of the generals. He hastily took some of the most barbarian of the archers and marched to Oenoe. This was an Athenian fort on the Boeotian border, which the Corinthians were besieging at that moment. They were angry at the loss of a party returning from Decelea, which the garrison had cut off. The Corinthians had volunteered for this service and had called on the Boeotians to help them. After consulting with the Boeotians, Aristarchus deceived the garrison in Oenoe. He told them that their countrymen in the city had come to terms with the Lacedaemonians, and that one of the terms of the surrender was that they must give up the place to the Boeotians. The garrison believed him, since he was a general and since the siege had kept them from knowing what had happened. So they evacuated the fort under truce. In this way the Boeotians gained possession of Oenoe, and the oligarchy and the troubles at Athens came to an end.

To return to the Peloponnesians in Miletus. No pay came from any of the agents whom Tissaphernes had appointed for the purpose when he left for Aspendus. Neither the Phoenician fleet nor Tissaphernes gave any sign of appearing. Philip, who had been sent with him, and another Spartan, Hippocrates, who was at Phaselis, wrote to Mindarus, the admiral, that the ships were not coming at all and that Tissaphernes was treating them shamefully. Meanwhile Pharnabazus was inviting them to come to him. He was making every effort to get the fleet and, like Tissaphernes, to bring about the revolt of the cities in his government that were still subject to Athens, and he had great hopes of success. At length, at about the point in the summer that we have now reached, Mindarus yielded to his urging. He weighed anchor at Miletus with seventy-three ships, in good order and at a moment’s notice, to elude the enemy at Samos, and set sail for the Hellespont. Sixteen vessels had already gone there ahead of him in the same summer and had overrun part of the Chersonese. Mindarus was caught in a storm and forced to put in at Icarus. After being held up there for five or six days by the weather, he arrived at Chios.

Meanwhile Thrasyllus heard that Mindarus had put out from Miletus. He immediately set sail from Samos with fifty-five ships, in haste to reach the Hellespont before him. But then he learned that Mindarus was at Chios, and he expected him to stay there. So he posted scouts in Lesbos and on the mainland opposite, to make sure the fleet could not move without his knowing it. He himself coasted along to Methymna and ordered meal and other necessaries to be prepared, so that he could attack from Lesbos if the enemy stayed at Chios for any length of time. In the meantime he resolved to sail against Eresus, a town in Lesbos that had revolted, and to take it if he could. Some of the leading Methymnian exiles had brought over about fifty heavy infantry from Cuma, their sworn associates. They hired others from the mainland, making three hundred in all, and chose Anaxander, a Theban, to command them, because the Thebans and the Lesbians were of the same blood. They first attacked Methymna. The Athenian guards advancing from Mitylene frustrated this attempt, and the exiles were repulsed a second time in a battle outside the city. They then crossed the mountain and brought about the revolt of Eresus. Thrasyllus therefore decided to go there with all his ships and attack the place. Thrasybulus had already gone ahead of him with five ships from Samos, as soon as he heard that the exiles had crossed over. He came too late to save Eresus, so he went on and anchored before the town. There they were also joined by two vessels on their way home from the Hellespont, and by the ships of the Methymnians, making a grand total of sixty-seven vessels. The forces on board now got ready, with engines and every other means available, to do their utmost to storm Eresus.

In the meantime Mindarus and the Peloponnesian fleet were at Chios. They took on provisions for two days, and the Chians gave each man three Chian pieces of money. On the third day they put out from the island in haste. To avoid meeting the ships at Eresus, they did not make for the open sea but kept Lesbos on their left and sailed toward the mainland. They touched at the port of Carteria, in the Phocaeid, and dined. Then they went on along the Cumaean coast and supped at Arginusae, on the mainland opposite Mitylene. From there they continued along the coast, although it was late in the night, and arrived at Harmatus on the mainland opposite Methymna, where they dined. They then passed swiftly by Lectum, Larisa, Hamaxitus and the neighboring towns, and arrived a little before midnight at Rhoeteum. Here they were now in the Hellespont. Some of the ships also put in at Sigeum and at other places in the neighborhood.

Meanwhile the eighteen Athenian ships at Sestos were warned of the approach of the Peloponnesian fleet by fire signals and by a sudden increase in the number of fires on the enemy’s shore. That very night they set sail in haste, just as they were. They hugged the shore of the Chersonese and coasted along to Elaeus, intending to sail out into the open sea, away from the enemy’s fleet.

They passed the sixteen ships at Abydos without being seen. Those ships had been warned by their approaching friends to stay alert and stop them from sailing out, but they failed to do so. At dawn the Athenians sighted the fleet of Mindarus, which immediately gave chase. They did not all have time to get away. The greater number escaped to Imbros and Lemnos, but four of the hindmost were overtaken off Elaeus. One of these was stranded opposite the temple of Protesilaus and taken with its crew. Two others were taken without their crews. The fourth was abandoned on the shore of Imbros and burned by the enemy.

After this the Peloponnesians were joined by the squadron from Abydos, which brought their fleet to a grand total of eighty-six vessels. They spent the day in an unsuccessful siege of Elaeus and then sailed back to Abydos. Meanwhile the Athenians were deceived by their scouts. They never dreamed that the enemy’s fleet could get by undetected, and they were besieging Eresus without alarm. As soon as they heard the news, they abandoned Eresus at once and made all speed for the Hellespont. On the way they took two of the Peloponnesian ships, which had been carried too far out into the open sea in the ardor of the pursuit and now fell in their way. The next day they dropped anchor at Elaeus. They brought back the ships that had taken refuge at Imbros, and for five days they prepared for the coming engagement.

After this they engaged in the following way. The Athenians formed in column and sailed close along the shore toward Sestos. When the Peloponnesians saw this, they put out from Abydos to meet them. Both sides realized that a battle was now at hand, and both extended their lines. The Athenians stretched along the Chersonese from Idacus to Arrhiani with seventy-six ships. The Peloponnesians stretched from Abydos to Dardanus with eighty-six. The Syracusans held the Peloponnesian right wing, and Mindarus in person held their left with the best sailers in the navy. Thrasyllus commanded the Athenian left and Thrasybulus their right, with the other commanders in different parts of the fleet. The Peloponnesians hurried to engage first. With their left they outflanked the Athenian right, and they tried to cut the Athenians off, if possible, from sailing out of the straits, and to drive their center onto the shore, which was not far off. The Athenians saw their intention and extended their own wing so as to outsail them, while their left had by this time passed the point of Cynossema. But this forced them to thin and weaken their center, especially as they had fewer ships than the enemy, and as the coast round Point Cynossema formed a sharp angle that prevented them from seeing what was going on on the other side of it.

The Peloponnesians now attacked the Athenian center, drove their ships ashore and disembarked to follow up their victory. The center could get no help from either wing. Thrasybulus on the right could not help, because of the number of ships attacking him. Thrasyllus on the left could not help either: the point of Cynossema hid what was going on, and he was also held back by his Syracusan and other opponents, whose numbers were fully equal to his own. At length, however, the Peloponnesians, confident of victory, began to scatter in pursuit of the enemy’s ships, and a considerable part of their fleet fell into disorder. When the squadron of Thrasybulus saw this, it stopped its lateral movement, faced about, and attacked and routed the ships opposed to it. Then it fell roughly on the scattered vessels of the victorious Peloponnesian division and put most of them to flight without a blow. By this time the Syracusans had also given way before the squadron of Thrasyllus, and when they saw the flight of their comrades they took openly to flight.

The rout was now complete. Most of the Peloponnesians fled first to the river Midius and afterward to Abydos. The Athenians took only a few ships, since the narrowness of the Hellespont meant that the enemy had not far to go to be safe. Nevertheless nothing could have been more timely for the Athenians than this victory. Up to this time they had feared the Peloponnesian fleet, because of a number of petty losses and the disaster in Sicily. Now they stopped distrusting themselves, and they no longer thought their enemies any good at sea. They took from the enemy eight Chian vessels, five Corinthian, two Ambraciot, two Boeotian, and one each of Leucadian, Lacedaemonian, Syracusan and Pellenian, and they lost fifteen of their own. They set up a trophy on Point Cynossema, secured the wrecks, gave the enemy back his dead under truce, and sent a galley to Athens with the news of their victory. This vessel brought good news that nobody had hoped for, coming after the recent disasters in Euboea and in the midst of the revolution at Athens. Its arrival gave the Athenians fresh courage, and made them believe that if they put their shoulders to the wheel their cause might yet prevail.

On the fourth day after the sea-fight, the Athenians in Sestos hastily refitted their ships and sailed against Cyzicus, which had revolted. Off Harpagium and Priapus they sighted the eight vessels from Byzantium at anchor. They sailed up, routed the troops on shore and took the ships. Then they went on and recovered the town of Cyzicus, which was unfortified, and levied money from the citizens. In the meantime the Peloponnesians sailed from Abydos to Elaeus. They recovered those of their captured galleys that were still undamaged, the rest having been burned by the Elaeusians, and sent Hippocrates and Epicles to Euboea to fetch the squadron from that island.

About the same time Alcibiades returned to Samos with his thirteen ships from Caunus and Phaselis. He brought word that he had kept the Phoenician fleet from joining the Peloponnesians, and that he had made Tissaphernes more friendly to the Athenians than before. Alcibiades now manned nine more ships and levied large sums of money from the Halicarnassians, and he fortified Cos. After doing this and placing a governor in Cos, he sailed back to Samos, as autumn was now at hand. Meanwhile Tissaphernes heard that the Peloponnesian fleet had sailed from Miletus to the Hellespont. He set off again from Aspendus and made all sail for Ionia. While the Peloponnesians were in the Hellespont, the Antandrians, a people of Aeolic extraction, brought some heavy infantry from Abydos by land across Mount Ida and let them into the town. They had been ill-treated by Arsaces, the Persian lieutenant of Tissaphernes. This same Arsaces, on the pretext of a secret quarrel, had invited the chief men of the Delians to undertake military service. (These were Delians who had settled at Atramyttium after the Athenians had driven them from their homes for the sake of purifying Delos.) He drew them out from their town as his friends and allies, lay in wait for them at dinner, surrounded them and had his soldiers shoot them down. This deed made the Antandrians fear that he might some day do them some harm. He also laid burdens on them that were too heavy for them to bear. So they expelled his garrison from their citadel.

Tissaphernes heard of this act of the Peloponnesians, in addition to what had happened at Miletus and Cnidus, where his garrisons had also been expelled. He now saw that the breach between them was serious. He feared further injury from them. He was also vexed to think that Pharnabazus should receive them, and might perhaps succeed better against Athens than he had done, in less time and at less cost. So he decided to rejoin them in the Hellespont, to complain of the events at Antandros and to excuse himself as best he could on the matter of the Phoenician fleet and the other charges against him. Accordingly he went first to Ephesus and offered sacrifice to Artemis....
[When the winter after this summer is over the twenty-first year of this war will be completed.]
